video_title: How Franchise Restaurants Opened the Door to the Gig Economy | Odd Lots
gist: Open Markets Institute chief economist Brian Callaci, author of 'Chains of Command: The Rise and Cruel Reign of the Franchise Economy,' explains to Tracy Alloway and Joe Weisenthal how a 1960s-70s antitrust-law rewrite let franchisors like McDonald's control nearly every aspect of a 'franchisee's business while offloading employer liability, how that same legal architecture underpins today's Uber and Amazon gig-worker classification, and how wage suppression remains the one lever franchisees can pull.

themes.theme: Franchise structure and the principal-agent problem

insights.claim: A franchise is legally simple: the franchisor licenses its trademark to a nominally independent franchisee for a royalty (typically 6-20% of sales), while dictating nearly every operational detail -- prices, hours, product mix, even how many seconds an employee has to greet a customer and which approved equipment (e.g., McDonald's ice cream machines) they may use -- making franchisees functionally 'middle managers with more risk' rather than true independent business owners.
insights.speaker: Brian Callaci, chief economist, Open Markets Institute
insights.so_what: Undercuts the 'entrepreneurship' marketing narrative used to recruit franchisees and gig workers -- a useful lens for evaluating any 'be your own boss' investment or labor-supply pitch.
insights.quote: a franchise or just like an entrepreneur makes the worst franchisee.

insights.claim: Franchising partly solves the principal-agent problem (an owner-operator with 'skin in the game' works harder than a salaried manager), but Callaci argues its bigger historical appeal to franchisors was legal: franchisees are classified as separate businesses rather than employees, so they don't qualify for overtime or minimum-wage protections and, until recently, had no clear legal path to unionize against the parent brand.
insights.speaker: Brian Callaci, chief economist, Open Markets Institute
insights.so_what: Highlights franchising as fundamentally a labor-cost-arbitrage legal structure, relevant to evaluating labor-cost and regulatory risk in any franchise-heavy public company.

insights.claim: The primary, and often only, lever a franchisee has to improve unit profitability is squeezing labor costs, because the franchisor controls nearly everything else, including staffing levels mandated in the operations manual, which the franchisor can unilaterally change at any time.
insights.speaker: Brian Callaci, chief economist, Open Markets Institute
insights.so_what: Direct investment implication: franchise-model profitability at the unit level is structurally tied to wage suppression, making labor-cost regulation (minimum wage hikes, joint-employer rules) a first-order risk factor for franchisors and franchisees alike.
insights.quote: the major lever that franchisees have, to be a better business to produce more money is to basically squeeze wage costs.

themes.theme: The 1960s-70s antitrust rewrite that legalized franchisor control

insights.claim: Franchisor control over pricing, territory, and products was illegal under 1960s-70s antitrust law, which treated it as an anti-competitive vertical restraint incompatible with the 'independent business owner' model; founders like Ray Kroc and Colonel Sanders, together with the newly formed International Franchise Association, ran a deliberate, self-acknowledged lobbying and litigation campaign -- aided by University of Chicago law-and-economics scholars -- to redefine antitrust doctrine so this control became legal under a 'rule of reason' standard.
insights.speaker: Brian Callaci, chief economist, Open Markets Institute
insights.so_what: Traces the specific legal-doctrine shift underlying today's platform and gig-economy legal architecture -- relevant background for assessing regulatory-reversal risk to gig and franchise business models.

insights.claim: In 1963 and 1965 Senate Antitrust Subcommittee hearings, the International Franchise Association's own president effectively conceded, under questioning, that franchisors sought 'vertical integration by other means' -- wanting full operational control without the legal liabilities of actually owning the business or employing the workers.
insights.speaker: Brian Callaci, chief economist, Open Markets Institute
insights.so_what: An original-source, citable historical admission of franchisor intent, useful for legal and regulatory risk analysis around misclassification litigation theories.
insights.quote: we're trying to get vertical integration by other means. We don't want to own the assets. We don't want to employ the workers. Those are risks we'd rather do without. We want the benefits of that control, but we really don't want to be held liable for it.

insights.claim: Franchise contracts historically included no-poaching clauses preventing workers at one location of a brand from being hired by another location of the same brand without the current franchisee's permission -- legal under antitrust's vertical/horizontal distinction (a franchisor-imposed no-poach is treated more leniently under 'rule of reason' than an illegal horizontal agreement between competitors) even though its wage-suppressing effect is economically identical.
insights.speaker: Brian Callaci, chief economist, Open Markets Institute
insights.so_what: Flags a well-documented anti-competitive labor practice that has drawn state attorney general and DOJ scrutiny in recent years -- relevant precedent for assessing labor-antitrust litigation risk in franchise-heavy sectors.

insights.claim: Callaci's research, exploiting a natural experiment where Washington state entered a consent decree with McDonald's and other chains eliminating no-poach clauses, found wages rose afterward -- a causal empirical finding that no-poach restrictions measurably suppressed franchise-worker wages.
insights.speaker: Brian Callaci, chief economist, Open Markets Institute
insights.so_what: Direct empirical evidence quantifying the wage impact of eliminating anti-competitive labor clauses -- relevant to modeling margin impact if similar consent decrees or FTC rules expand nationally.

insights.claim: Research cited by Callaci (David Weil's 'The Fissured Workplace' and earlier work by Alan Krueger) finds that even within the same brand, workers at company-owned locations earn higher wages and have better long-term wage/promotion trajectories than workers at franchised locations of the identical chain, and franchised locations have measurably higher rates of workplace-safety and other labor-law violations.
insights.speaker: Brian Callaci, chief economist, Open Markets Institute
insights.so_what: A concrete, sourced wage and violation gap between corporate-owned and franchised units -- a useful comparative metric for labor-risk screening of franchise-heavy restaurant and retail companies.

insights.claim: Callaci and colleagues hand-coded 530 franchise contracts over 18 months, drawing on public records made available under a 1979 FTC rule requiring franchise disclosure documents filed in certain states like Wisconsin and California; follow-up research using text-scraping tools has since found franchise contracts have become measurably more restrictive over the past 20 years.
insights.speaker: Brian Callaci, chief economist, Open Markets Institute
insights.so_what: Identifies an underused public-record dataset (state-filed FDDs) and a documented, worsening trend in contractual restrictiveness -- a leading indicator for labor-cost and regulatory risk in franchise-sector investments.

themes.theme: From franchising to the gig economy

insights.claim: Callaci argues the legal architecture gig-economy platforms like Uber and Amazon's 'Delivery Service Partner' program use to classify workers as independent contractors is a direct descendant of the franchise antitrust victories of the 1960s-70s, arguing Amazon's DSP model is even closer to a franchise than Uber, since DSP operators are small incorporated companies (running, say, 30 trucks) rather than individual driver-entrepreneurs, with Amazon reportedly fronting some capital while keeping drivers legally employed by the DSP rather than by Amazon.
insights.speaker: Brian Callaci, chief economist, Open Markets Institute
insights.so_what: A direct legal-lineage argument connecting franchise case law to gig-platform liability shielding -- relevant for assessing misclassification and liability litigation risk at Amazon, Uber, or similar platforms.

insights.claim: Unlike a traditional vertically-integrated manufacturer such as 1950s US Steel or General Motors, which had comparatively less granular real-time control over its own directly-employed workforce, McDonald's today -- despite employing hardly anyone directly -- exercises tighter operational control over its franchisees via continuous point-of-sale and broadband data feeds since the 1990s, and now AI-based worker-level surveillance able to flag a specific slow employee by name to the franchisee.
insights.speaker: Brian Callaci, chief economist, Open Markets Institute
insights.so_what: Highlights how real-time data and AI dramatically increase the degree of practical operational control corporations can exert without a formal employment relationship -- an important framework for evaluating 'control without liability' risk in any modern platform business, not just restaurants.
insights.quote: McDonald's now hardly employs anybody, but they have way more control because they're able to get that, that stream of data.

insights.claim: Domino's imposes a 30-minute delivery guarantee that pressures drivers to speed, yet if a driver rushing to meet that corporate-mandated deadline causes an accident, liability legally falls on the franchisee or driver rather than Domino's corporate.
insights.speaker: Brian Callaci, chief economist, Open Markets Institute
insights.so_what: A concrete illustrative case of 'control without liability' exposure -- relevant precedent for tort and liability-risk analysis in franchise and delivery-driven business models.

themes.theme: Policy, private equity, and the regulatory pendulum

insights.claim: Callaci's proposed policy fix is not to ban franchising or centralized corporate control -- he acknowledges real efficiency benefits from coordinated, centrally-planned corporate structures -- but to tie legal employer obligations and liabilities directly to whichever entity exercises real operational control, regardless of contractual labels.
insights.speaker: Brian Callaci, chief economist, Open Markets Institute
insights.so_what: A clear, actionable regulatory framework that, if adopted via new joint-employer rules or legislation, would directly raise labor costs and liability exposure for franchisors and gig platforms -- relevant for scenario-planning regulatory risk in these sectors.

insights.claim: Historically, private equity primarily bought franchise brands themselves -- the capital-light, high-margin, royalty-collecting franchisor entity, with Burger King cited as a famous example -- but Callaci notes a newer trend of private equity also acquiring and consolidating franchise operator businesses, including multi-unit and even multi-brand franchisee groups.
insights.speaker: Brian Callaci, chief economist, Open Markets Institute
insights.so_what: Flags a structural shift worth tracking for restaurant-sector PE investors: growing consolidation of franchisee operating companies (not just franchisor brands) changes labor-cost and consolidation dynamics at the unit-operator level.

insights.claim: Under the 1947 Taft-Hartley Act, franchise workers are legally barred from striking, picketing, or targeting the franchisor corporation directly and can only target their 'immediate employer' (the local franchisee); a 2010s Obama-era 'joint employer' NLRB rule briefly made it easier for workers to compel franchisor-level bargaining, but it was rescinded under Trump, restored under Biden, then reversed again, leaving the legal status of franchise-worker collective bargaining unsettled today.
insights.speaker: Brian Callaci, chief economist, Open Markets Institute
insights.so_what: Flags the 'joint employer' rule status as a specific, binary, politically-toggled regulatory variable that materially changes franchisor labor-cost and liability exposure depending on the administration in power -- a recurring pendulum to track at each administration change.

insights.claim: Contrasted with franchised chains like Dunkin' Donuts and Taco Bell, fully corporate-owned chains like Starbucks and Chipotle pay measurably higher wages and have allowed workers to at least vote for unionization (Starbucks) in ways franchise workers structurally have not, suggesting some of the rents generated by centralized corporate control can be shared with workers when the parent company is the direct employer.
insights.speaker: Brian Callaci, chief economist, Open Markets Institute
insights.so_what: Gives a clean comparison set (corporate-owned vs. franchised chains) investors and analysts can use to benchmark labor-cost and union risk differences within the restaurant sector.
